chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
title: Copying for Duke and Juan Tizol's refusal
summary: Whaley says too much copying ruined his eyes, and Hinton calls him the one copyist who could read Duke's handwriting, after Tizol.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: He didn't say it was because of drinking, did he.

No. I know what it was. Too much work. That's strain. I used to sit in Duke's home and he'd sit there writing and then we'd go down to the rehearsal hall where they're going to record and I would start copying it and by the time he had finished one number I had another number there ready for him.

You're the most, in the annals of jazz and orchestration, especially in the black society, you were known as the most famous copyist because you knew Duke's will, you knew his mind, you knew what he intended. Nobody else could read his copy but you. His henscratching.
What's his name, the trombone player, the Spanish guy.

Juan Tizol, he did the copying before I come in there, see and Juan said no, I ain't going blind copying Duke's music. Well, I never had that -- no, I never thought about going blind because the woman doctor had told me I had good eye and I used to go up to the medical center there at 153rd Street and the man used to give me drops for it. But it seemed like it went, I overstrained it.
